claims.claim: Reviewers describe the combat mechanics as clunky, stiff, and lacking responsiveness, with inconsistent parrying and dodging.

citations.review_text: If you enjoyed any other souls-like, you'll be disappointed by this. Combat is a clunky janky mess. The devs didn't realise that if you want to make a hard game that's fun, the combat has to be responsive. PC frame rates and frame pacing are also awful. Just don't bother with this game, there are plenty of others.

I was really excited for this game when it got announced and I decided to finally give it a try. 

First, I was really unhappy with the Umbral mechanics. If your disdain for tedium isn't motivation enough to stay out of Umbral, the game incentivizes you to stay out of it because it serves as a "second chance" if you die. Having to enter Umbral and interact with a movement node to pull a platform towards you then with another node to move the platform forward a few feet then another node to move it another few feet, is far from an engaging way to delve into the world and interact with the environment. Bloated with "function" and devoid of meaningful impact to the game is how I would describe Umbral.

Second, I did like the faster pace of combat compared to a typical Souls or Souls-like game. However, the parrying seemed really inconsistent (perhaps a skill issue) and when you did land enough of them it didn't seem to have enough of an effect on the fight to be worth it. Also dashing vs dodging seemed very pointless when dashing seemed to be sufficient for getting away from enemy attacks. This reflects the overall design language of this game of having things just to have them.

Finally, even two and a half years later the game just feels unpolished. I turned the master volume down to 3 to match my system as soon as I was able only to find that the cutscenes were unaffected! That hurt. When I tried to turn the master below 3 or any of the other volumes below 77 they would just go completely silent, and if they weren't at 100 the audio would cut in and out. There were also many times while running around that I could just walk over gaps or off of a ledge and turn around without consequence. Maybe this was intentional to provide a more forgiving exploration experience but it felt very odd to me.

This game really nails it's aesthetic/vibe which set it apart for me initially from other Souls-likes, and the story seemed interesting enough but with how it actually feels to…

citations.review_text: Firstly the game does run well and gameplay does mostly feel fun, it looks great, and compared to Fromsoft, this game actually has a story that gets told to you instead of being a book read through many different items. Although I did refund it I will still recommend the game based on if you like souls-likes, but do be warned that enemies in this game do have massive windups so you'll know that an attack is coming but split second attacks that make parrying a major struggle to do. I ask the devs to please look into balancing this and fixing the tutorial on activation of popups for things as I had to fumble around and figure out the controls and what many things do on my own because the popups wouldn't show till after I had already figured it out.

Played this game on my XBSX with GamePass and got way further in than on Steam. It ran horribly on XBOX, to the point where I couldn't play in some areas, but I still wanted to give it a chance. Got it on PC recently, hoping it would run better than on the console but nope, still chugging like crazy whenever there are just a bit too many particle effects on-screen. I'm running most contemporary game on max settings, 1080p at 60 FPS and above.

Played and completed all major Souls and Souls-like games on the market, multiple times for some, and I can subjectively say that Lords of the Fallen has the worst gameplay out of all of them. Even Code Vein 1 which I also disliked has smoother movement and animations. Enemy attack timings and patterns are some of the most chaotic I've seen, thrown out randomly with little to no telegraphing and just feel like thrown in for the sake of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ difficulty.

The setting and story are so generic that I have no interest in reading any of the lore on the items. The writing wants to be epic and edgy, but it just ends up as cringy and trying way too hard to be esoteric and like in other Souls-games.

I may give it another try in the future when I have nothing else to play or I'm feeling bored and in a Souls mood.

The enemy movement in this game is not telegraphed well and that makes combat unenjoyable. Also all that umbral stuff does not add anything interesting and is just annoying. 

I do look forward to next game though, art direction and sound design is very good, here's hoping they will figure it out.

Lords of the Fallen is a game with many ambitious ideas. It is not a perfect experience, but it has its own identity and several impressive designs that make it stand out.
The first thing that impressed me was the world design. The interconnected areas, shortcuts, and hidden paths create a strong sense of exploration. Many locations are connected in clever ways, making the world feel like a complete place rather than a collection of separate levels. Discovering a familiar area from another perspective always gives a satisfying feeling.
The Umbral world is also one of the game’s most unique features. The ability to shift between two different worlds changes both exploration and combat. The dark atmosphere, disturbing creatures, and religious themes create a strong sense of mystery and oppression throughout the journey.
However, the game also has some weaknesses. Some enemy encounters feel repetitive, and certain areas rely too much on enemy density rather than interesting combat situations. While the bosses often have impressive designs and atmosphere, some fights lack variety and deeper mechanics, making them less memorable than they could have been.
Despite these flaws, Lords of the Fallen shows a lot of creativity and passion. Its world, atmosphere, and unique mechanics demonstrate that the developers wanted to create something with its own identity instead of simply following a formula.
Overall, Lords of the Fallen is a flawed but interesting action RPG. It has moments of brilliance, especially in exploration and world building, even though some parts of the combat design could have been refined further. It is a journey through a beautiful but cruel world, filled with darkness, mystery, and ambition.

Lords of the Fallen is a game with many ambitious ideas. It is not a perfect experience, but it has its own identity and several impressive designs that make it stand out.
The first thing that impressed me was the world design. The interconnected areas, shortcuts, and hidden paths create a strong sense of exploration. Many locations are connected in clever ways, making the world feel like a complete place rather than a collection of separate levels. Discovering a familiar area from another perspective always gives a satisfying feeling.
The Umbral world is also one of the game’s most unique features. The ability to shift between two different worlds changes both exploration and combat. The dark atmosphere, disturbing creatures, and religious themes create a strong sense of mystery and oppression throughout the journey.
However, the game also has some weaknesses. Some enemy encounters feel repetitive, and certain areas rely too much on enemy density rather than interesting combat situations. While the bosses often have impressive designs and atmosphere, some fights lack variety and deeper mechanics, making them less memorable than they could have been.
Despite these flaws, Lords of the Fallen shows a lot of creativity and passion. Its world, atmosphere, and unique mechanics demonstrate that the developers wanted to create something with its own identity instead of simply following a formula.
Overall, Lords of the Fallen is a flawed but interesting action RPG. It has moments of brilliance, especially in exploration and world building, even though some parts of the combat design could have been refined further. It is a journey through a beautiful but cruel world, filled with darkness, mystery, and ambition.

250+ hours later, I can confidently recommend Lords of the Fallen.


This isn't a perfect game.

I didn’t much like the 2014 “Prequel” and avoided the game at launch, thinking it be roughly the same. It isn’t, but I don’t regret starting playing with version 2.5. From what I heard, this LotF launched rough, some questlines are unnecessarily fragile, multiplayer can be quirky, and there are still moments where you'll wonder, "Who thought this was a good idea?"

Yet somehow...

I kept coming back.

What started as "I'll probably do one playthrough to wean myself of Mortal Shell" turned into hundreds of hours, multiple endings, PvP, build experimentation, and one of the most memorable Soulslike experiences I've had in years.

The combat has weight. Grand weapons feel appropriately devastating, shields are genuinely useful, and the weapon variety allows very different playstyles. I ended up falling in love with builds I never expected to enjoy.
The world is another highlight. Axiom and in particular Umbral are more than just a gimmick—they fundamentally change how you explore, think about level design, and discover secrets. Even after hundreds of hours I was still finding things I hadn't seen before. That is a big, perhaps the biggest selling point of a good souls game—it has to have something that inspires you to pay ATTENTION, be it the world, the lore, gameplay or philosophy. 

Surprisingly, one of my favorite parts became PvP. Not because it's perfectly balanced—it isn't—but because it created memorable stories. Rivals you start recognizing, tense duels, unexpected moments of sportsmanship, and those rare fights where both players clearly know exactly what they're doing. Those are the moments that stay with me far longer than any particular weapon or armor set.

That said, the game isn't without frustrations.

Quest progression is often far too easy to fail without realizing it, sometimes only discovering the consequences dozens of hours later. If you're aiming for …

This was my first Soulslike, and I went in knowing I may get destroyed, and want to move on after a few hours. Instead, it became my first ever 100% game on Steam.

Is the game perfect? No. Some questlines are easy to mess up without a guide, the story can be confusing at times, and farming the last few armor pieces definitely tested my patience. Even so, I had an absolute blast from start to finish.

The combat feels great, the world is beautiful, and the Umbral mechanic is one of the coolest ideas I've seen in a game. Getting 100% requires multiple playthroughs, but I honestly never got tired of replaying it. Every run gave me a reason to come back, whether it was trying a new build, completing another quest, or going for a different ending. And of course... all hail the Bucketlord.

More than anything, this game was a great introduction to the Souls genre. It made me understand why so many people love these games, and now I'm genuinely excited to dive deeper into the genre and experience more of the games that inspired Lords of the Fallen.

I can't wait for the sequel. If the developers build on this foundation and smooth out the rough edges, I think they'll have something really special.

For my first Soulslike and my first 100% completion, I couldn't have picked a better game.

Recommended.

A great entry into the Soulslike genre. The heavy metal aesthetics pulled me in from the very first trailer so I was tremendously disappointed to see the that it did not stick the landing on release. So many games fail to understand what makes a Soulslike special - even FromSoft fumbles when Miyazaki is not heading a project, as evidenced by Dark Souls 2 - and this was no exception. What this game did with that feedback, however, is why I want to sing its praise.

The gaming industry is at a low point right now with corporate greed and lack of passion creating unplayable flop one after another. What this smaller studio did after failing to impress gamers was to work tireless to tweak every possible element of the game in response to feedback. From stats, to enemy placements, to entire boss fights being reworked. Nothing was more impressive than for them to completely overhaul the co-op to go from the traditional "phone a friend" FromSoft style of Co-op and replace that with a one-to-one Shared progress co-op so you and a friend can enjoy the same instance from start to finish.

There is still plenty to criticize in this game, the weapons feel clunkier than they could be, some enemies are still arbitrarily hard, item drop rates are non existent. The weakest point, by far, are the quests; they took the FromSoft style of being vague and letting the player figure it out and misinterpreted that to mean making quests as backward and incomprehensible as possible. Kukajin and the Tortured Prisoner quests come to mind but there are others.

The visuals are a metalhead's dream come true, taking catholic grimdark to levels even more extravagant than Warhammer, and the art of the world is where this game truly shines. The unique feature of the Umbral Lamp and an entire secondary shadow world layered over the main world that you can jump in and out of is another key feature that makes this game stand out from others in the genre. It's no Elden Ring but it is worth your attention…

Despite running into a few bugs here and there and dealing with the incredibly tedious grind required to reach 100% completion, I still had an absolute blast with Lords of the Fallen.

What stood out to me most was the game's overall design. The world is stunning, dark, and atmospheric, with environments that constantly made me want to explore every corner. The weapon variety is fantastic, the armor sets look amazing, and the art direction as a whole is easily one of the game's strongest qualities. Building different characters and experimenting with gear never got old because everything feels so visually distinct and well-crafted.

The dual-world mechanic adds a unique layer to exploration, and discovering secrets hidden throughout the world was consistently rewarding. Combat is satisfying, build diversity is excellent, and the game offers plenty of content for players who enjoy diving deep into its systems.

Is it perfect? No. There were some bugs during my playthrough, and completionists should be prepared for a long and sometimes frustrating road to 100%. But even with those issues, the amount of fun I had far outweighed the negatives.

If you're a fan of soulslike games and appreciate incredible world design, memorable armor and weapon aesthetics, and rewarding exploration, Lords of the Fallen is absolutely worth playing. I spent 127 hours in it for a reason.

I tried Lords of the Fallen when it first came out, but I was put off by the gameplay being generally unpolished. I forgot about it for a while until the sequel was announced, which looks so damn good I decided to give the first another chance.
I'm now on my fourth playthrough.
I am genuinely impressed with how much the devs have listened to feedback and improved the game. It is now a great Soulslike with everything I love about the genre: tight combat, excellent variety of weapons and spells, and builds, builds, builds! The addition of unlockable classes enhances the replayability even more.
I only have two major gripes. Enemy variety is a well-known issue, and while I don't think it hampers the enjoyment too much, it's still noteworthy. My biggest annoyance are the ambushes. Every Souls game has them, but nowhere near this many. If enemies aren't waiting behind corners waiting to shove you off a ledge, then they're sneaking up behind you with little to no audio cues to alert you. It gets very, very old.
Even still, I highly recommend Lords of the Fallen, and I'm very excited for the sequel!

I would like to give this game a mixed option but since Steam refuses that to add that option, I instead actually do not recommend this game. It is one of the most confused games I have ever played, especially after reading through a lot of the update changes it has had since the extremely rough launch back in 2023. This game has a lot misdirected passion, most notably in the combat and exploration side of things. It takes elements from Sekiro for the posture system, Fromsoftware's catalouge in general for interconnected level design and gank fest enemy placement, and the plain "punish the player" trend most games are leaning on these days. I actually am excited for the lords of the Fallen 2 coming out in 2027, because you can see the developers are still very passionate and dedicated to this series for some reason. There are so many little design choices this game makes that drive me crazy; but instead of telling you the bad things the game does like many other reviews, I will instead share things I genuinely like instead.

The art direction is great. I love the moody atmosphere and chunky armor and really fun zealot enemy design. I do wish they had a bigger variety instead of palette swaps, however they do them well despite that.

The combat system is terrible and clunky, but I do like that you can dual wield most weapons together, even it is very inconsistent with damage and hit-boxes. citations.review_text: I played the game at launch and ended up dropping it before finishing. It was pretty frustrating back then. Lots of bugs, insane and unnecessary mob density, and maps that were way too dark. :3  However, I always believed the core concept was really cool. Fast forward to the 2.5 patch, and it completely turned the game around. The combat feels much more polished, bosses are more fair and fun, and the replay value is excellent. I just don’t get tired of playing it.  My only real complaint nowadays is the target lock-on. Sometimes I try to lock onto the enemy right in front of me and the game decides to lock onto some random mob halfway across the map. It’s absurd and annoying, but at this point I just laugh at it. xD Aside from that minor issue, the game is worth every penny in 2026. Highly recommended! :D

While I do recommend this game, I do so with the caveat of not going to NG+ if you can help it. Wonky hitboxes and big damage numbers make things quite annoying.
